name: Komo
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 1 other work consulted does not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Otero, Manuel A. 2019. A Historical Reconstruction of the Koman Language Family. PhD dissertation, University of Oregon (ScholarsBank handle 1794/25239).
catalog_quote: Komo displays three level tones – (L)ow, (M)id and (H)igh – as well as (R)ising and (F)alling contour tones. Minimal tone pairs are seen in (13). The level and contour tones can occur on a single vowel nucleus though contour tones can result from two vowel nuclei of differing level tones coming together at a morpheme boundary. ... Overall, tone is quite stable in Komo: there is no evidence of downstep or downdrift in prosodic words or even across longer sentences. The functional load of tone is moderate in the lexicon, more present in the verbal system where tonal suppletion in verb roots is a means of distinguishing nominal and verbal number. ... There are four main tone classes for monosyllabic roots ... The four root-level tone classes are H, M, L1 and L2.

tone_statements.citation: Otero, Manuel A. (2013). Aspects of Ethiopian Komo (morpho)phonology. Linguistic Discovery 16. pp. 136-178.
tone_statements.quote: Komo displays three level tones as well as rising and falling contour tones. Overall, tone is quite stable in Komo: there is no evidence of downstep or downdrift in prosodic words or even across longer sentences and virtually every underlying tone and tone melody surfaces faithfully. The functional load of tone is moderate in the lexicon, more present in the verbal system where verbs can be subcategorized into classes by their tonal behavior. Further, many verb roots can also be tonally suppletive in number. [...] Burns (1947) claims there are four level tones in Sudanese Komo but I find no evidence, either phonetic or phonological, to support this in Ethiopian Komo. The current analysis proposes three level tones: (L)ow, (M)id and (H)igh.

audit.reasoning: Quote confirmed verbatim at the stated pages in the held Otero 2019 dissertation; the held dedicated phonology article (Otero 2018, Linguistic Discovery) independently gives the same three-level-tone system with all nine melodies on disyllables and no stress/accent statement, so 'tonal' (tonal-OR-pitch accent, stress unstated) with domain not stated by the source is the right reading of the best modern sources, both by the principal fieldworker. The only unheld work that could add a stress statement is Tesfaye Negash 2015 (435-pp AAU grammar), which is not openly retrievable (ELAR login; absent from AAU ETD) and whose phonology Otero characterises as cursory; it would at most refine, not overturn, a tone-system coding. no reclassification or identity issue (record correctly concerns Koman Komo komo1258, not Bantu Komo komo1260 of Thomas 1992).
